Right to Be Forgotten After Acquittal: How the Cartabia Reform Works in Practice

By RMA — Web Reputation Agency

If an Italian criminal proceeding against you ended in acquittal, a judgment of no grounds to proceed or a dismissal (archiviazione), you can ask the court registry to add an annotation to the decision under art. 64-ter of the implementing provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure. That annotation, introduced by the Riforma Cartabia, is the formal basis for asking Google and other search engines to deindex news that links your name to the case.

What art. 64-ter changed for people cleared in court

Before the reform, anyone seeking the right to be forgotten after acquittal in Italy had to build the case from scratch, arguing relevance and the passage of time against the public interest in the news. The right to be forgotten Cartabia mechanism gives that person a document issued by the judicial authority itself, which search engines cannot easily dismiss.

The rule, added by Legislative Decree 150/2022 and in force since 30 December 2022, provides two distinct annotations that the registry (cancelleria) affixes to the decision:

  • Preclusion of indexing – a note stating that, within the limits of art. 17 GDPR, the indexing of the decision itself on the internet through search engines using your personal data is precluded. This protects against future publication of the ruling.
  • Removal of indexing – a note stating that the decision constitutes a title to obtain, under art. 17 GDPR, the removal from search engine indexing of online content concerning the criminal proceedings and containing your data. This is the one that matters for articles already online.

You can request one or both. In practice, most people with existing press coverage ask for the second, because it targets newspaper articles, blog posts and aggregator pages rather than the judgment.

Who is entitled to request the annotation

The request belongs to the person in whose favour the decision was issued: the former suspect or defendant, directly or through a lawyer. Victims, witnesses or relatives named in the same proceedings are not covered by this specific tool and must rely on the ordinary art. 17 GDPR route.

Decisions that qualify

The norm refers to judgments of proscioglimento, judgments of non luogo a procedere and orders of archiviazione. Proscioglimento covers full acquittal on the merits and also "non doversi procedere" outcomes; how registries and search engines treat dismissals for statute of limitations is less settled, so those cases deserve a careful assessment before filing.

Decisions that do not qualify

Convictions, plea agreements (patteggiamento) and penal decrees fall outside art. 64-ter, even if the sentence was later extinguished. People in that position may still pursue deindexing under the general balancing test, but without the advantage of the court annotation. A mixed outcome, acquittal on some charges and conviction on others, generally does not support a clean annotation on the whole case.

How to request the annotation from the court registry

The request is a short written application filed with the registry of the judge who issued the decision: the tribunal or appeal court for judgments, the office of the judge for preliminary investigations (GIP) for dismissals.

  1. Obtain a copy of the decision and, where relevant, a certificate that it is no longer subject to appeal; registries generally expect the outcome to be stable before annotating it.
  2. Draft the application citing art. 64-ter disp. att. c.p.p., specifying whether you request preclusion, removal of indexing, or both.
  3. File it in person, by certified email (PEC) or through the lawyer's electronic filing channel, depending on the practice of the specific court in Milan, Rome or elsewhere.
  4. Collect a certified copy of the decision bearing the annotation; this copy, not the bare judgment, is what you will submit to search engines.

Timing varies widely between courts. Some registries annotate within days, others take weeks, especially for older files held in archives. A polite follow-up with the file number usually speeds things up more than a formal reminder.

From the court annotation to deindexing on Google

The annotated decision does not reach Google automatically: you still need to file a personal information removal request listing every URL. The difference is that the request now rests on a judicial title rather than on your own arguments alone, which is the practical core of deindexing after an acquittal in Italy.

Building the Google request

Use Google's EU privacy removal form, list each URL that appears for searches of your name, attach the annotated decision and briefly explain that each page reports the criminal proceedings that ended in your favour. Searches combining your name with your town or profession often surface additional pages worth including. Google still performs its own assessment, but an annotation under art. 64-ter carries considerable weight in that review.

Other search engines

Bing and other engines operating in the EU have their own forms under art. 17 GDPR. Filing with all of them avoids the common situation in which an article disappears from Google but remains visible elsewhere, and in AI answers that draw on those indexes.

For a broader view of how name-based delisting operates, including its typical limits, see our article on the deindexing mechanism and its concrete limits.

What the annotation does not do

Deindexing removes the link between your name and the content in search results; it does not delete the article. The page remains on the newspaper's website and can be found by searching other terms, such as the case or the company involved.

The Cartabia annotation opens the door to delisting; it does not oblige a publisher to delete or rewrite its archive.

Two complementary steps often make sense. The first is asking the publisher to update the article with the outcome, a request consistent with Italian case law on keeping online archives accurate. The second is asking for anonymisation of your name where the story keeps some public value but your identity no longer does. Neither is guaranteed, and both work better when presented calmly with the annotated decision attached.

If the request is refused or partly accepted

Search engines sometimes accept certain URLs and reject others, for instance when an article also covers a public role you still hold. A partial refusal can be challenged by a reasoned resubmission, a complaint to the Garante per la protezione dei dati personali, or a claim before the ordinary court.

Before escalating, review whether the rejected pages actually concern the acquitted proceedings or other events, and whether your current public role has changed the balance.
